newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Sierra Leone says Liberians behind coup leaders.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone says Liberians behind coup leaders.

text.p: Sierre Leone's U.N. ambassador on Wednesday accused Liberians of proping up the coup leaders that ousted the country's elected government.

"The evidence is very clear that those in charge today in Sierra Leone are not those ill-considered military people who have made a coup," said James Jonah, a former senior U.N. official and advisor to ousted President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
Instead he said the rebel Revolutionary United Front (RUF) prevented the army coup leaders from being flexible in dealing with international demands they give up power.
"The control has passed on to the RUF, which is today controlled by Liberians," Jonah told a news conference. "They are digging in their heels."

Sierra Leone's civilian government was overthrown on May 25 in a coup led by non-commissioned military officers, who then formed an alliance with the RUF, which had fought the government in 1991 after years in the countryside. The new government has not been recognised by any country or the United Nations.
Jonah said his exiled government did not want to wage war on Liberia, itself recovering from years of lawlessness, but to return to civilian rule.

Foreign ministers from the Economic Community of West African States, meeting on June 26 in Guinea's capital of Conakry, where Kabbah is in exile, decided to enter into a dialogue and use economic sanctions to persuade the coup leaders to step down.
But they also retained the option of military force should mediators from Nigeria, Ghana, Guinea, the Ivory Coast and the Organisation of African Unity make no headway.

Jonah said the coup leaders "seem to be missing the point" and believed that negotiations would take place whereas the African leaders were attempting to clear the way for a return to civilian rule in the former British colony.

"The government of President Kabbah seeks no wider war. Nor does it intend to wage a war of revenge against the RUF or the army," he said. "The main objective of the legal government is to make it abundantly clear than an act of treason should not be allowed to succeed."

Jonah went back to Sierra Leone after years as a U.N. undersecretary-general to become chairman of an electoral commission. In March 1996, he managed to convince people to vote in large numbers despite threats from the RUF which opposed the poll that resulted in Kabbah's election.
